name: Henry Kissinger
role: US National Security Adviser (1969–1975) and Secretary of State (1973–1977)
summary: A realist in foreign policy who held that international order rests on a balance of power joined to legitimacy, and who favoured negotiated great-power arrangements over ideological crusades. He drove détente, the opening to China and arms limitation, and also backed covert and military action (Chile, Cambodia, Kurds). Most of his writing concerns foreign affairs, so his positions on domestic economy and society are largely unrecorded.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In October 2023 he criticised large-scale immigration into Germany, as reported in his biography; he did not set out a specific policy of reduction.

nation-first.rationale: He grounded order in states' realistic assessments of national interest and praised Sadat for peacemaking on that basis, and criticised foreign policy that dismisses national interest; he also favoured cooperation among great powers, so the answer is mixed.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: He did not rule out humanitarian aims but argued that a humanitarian foreign policy as central operating concept raises dilemmas and that the statesman must balance security and values case by case; his record includes both interventions and refusals to act on human-rights grounds.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: World Order asks whether networked technology will bring community or a world 'without limits or order, careening through crises without comprehending them', and warns of nuclear proliferation; he does not expect technology alone to solve problems.

democracy-best.rationale: World Order says Western tradition requires support for democratic institutions and free elections, but that elections can yield a single democratic exercise and that the statesman must balance security against promoting legitimate governance; he supported both democratic and autocratic partners.

political-violence-never.rationale: Record: in 1970 he backed a push for a military coup to stop Allende's inauguration, and later supported the Chilean and Argentine juntas; he gave no general statement on political violence.

military-superiority.rationale: In 1957 he wanted an adequate retaliatory force and warned against equating superiority with resources; in office he accepted rough parity with the USSR in SALT I.

results-over-ideology.rationale: His practice and writing put assessed realities and interests ahead of ideology: détente with Moscow, the opening to China, and World Order's statement that Western foreign policy success depends on assessing existing realities and trends.

universal-morality.rationale: Inferred: he defined legitimacy in order as acceptance by the major powers and not as justice, and set public opinion and morality aside; he stressed that civilisations hold different concepts of order.

force-without-un.rationale: He supported the 2003 Iraq invasion (World Order: 'I supported the decision to undertake regime change in Iraq'), which had no explicit Security Council authorisation, and drove the Cambodia operations without UN approval.

national-mission.rationale: He wrote that spreading American values by example and civil assistance is honoured, but that seeking to achieve them by military occupation proved beyond what the American public and Iraqi society could accommodate; he cautioned against making humanitarian or democratising aims the central operating concept of strategy.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Record: he cancelled a US warning to Chile against political assassinations and is reported to have worked to thwart Carter-era efforts to indict Chilean agents over the Letelier killing.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He sought to revitalise NATO and argued in 2023 for admitting Ukraine; World Order treats the Atlantic partnership as a pillar of order and asks how it should be given new meaning.

collective-defense.rationale: Throughout his career he worked to strengthen NATO (the 1973 'Year of Europe' initiative); in 2023 he said Ukraine should be inside NATO. World Order describes the Atlantic Alliance as resting on the US nuclear guarantee to Europe.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Contested: in 2016 he advised accepting Crimea as Russian, and in May 2022 he urged Ukraine to cede territory to restore the pre-invasion lines; he did not discuss the general legal status of annexation.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: On Iraq he wrote that democracy was pursued by occupation 'in a part of the world where they had no historical roots' and that this could not be expected to work in a politically relevant time; World Order also stresses that other civilizations hold different concepts of order.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: In May 1972 he agreed to the Shah's plan to back Kurdish peshmerga against Iraq's Ba'athist government; he also backed covert action against Allende in 1970.

democratic-peace.rationale: World Order presents the idea that democracy spread brings peace as the prevailing American view, contrasted with the European balance-of-power approach, and argues that its enforcement by occupation in Iraq failed.

non-intervention.rationale: His record is repeated intervention in other states' affairs: he drove the 1970 effort to block Allende's inauguration, backed Kurdish rebels against Iraq in 1972 and, in World Order, wrote that he supported the decision to undertake regime change in Iraq.

defeat-communism.rationale: As Nixon's adviser and secretary of state he pursued détente, SALT I and the ABM treaty with the Soviet Union and opened relations with China, rather than a policy of defeating communism. (His 1957 book distrusted Soviet 'peaceful coexistence' as tactic.)

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: He backed alignment with the Western alliance and, in 2023, Ukrainian NATO membership rather than neutrality; his 1957 book treats neutralism as the product of Western weakness.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He directed offensive operations beyond defence of the US (the 1969 bombing of Cambodia, which he came to support) and wrote in World Order that he supported regime change in Iraq in 2003.

arms-reduction.rationale: He negotiated SALT I and the ABM treaty, but wrote in 1957 that reducing forces had proved nearly impossible to negotiate and its rewards questionable, and in World Order that lower agreed levels can reduce stability.

open-diplomacy.rationale: His record includes secret diplomacy: the July 1971 secret trip to Beijing and confidential back channels with Moscow and Hanoi.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: In 1957 he wrote that the US 'must maintain at all times an adequate retaliatory force' and criticised its earlier unilateral disarmament; in World Order he treats mutual assured destruction as the mechanism of nuclear peace, and his SALT/ABM record limited rather than abolished arsenals.

national-resource-control.rationale: In 1974 he accepted Peru's sovereign right to nationalise property for public purposes, with compensation; this recognises national control over resources, not a general position.

multipolar-world.rationale: He favoured an equilibrium among several major powers: triangular diplomacy with Moscow and Beijing, and in World Order a global order built from American idealism plus traditional balance of power. He also warned against proliferation shifting the balance.

notes:
Domestic, economic and social statements are null: his books and the sources opened are almost wholly about foreign policy and strategy. Several of his later books and op-eds (Diplomacy, On China, Years of Upheaval, the 2014 Washington Post Ukraine piece, the 2020 WSJ piece, the 2023 Economist interview) were not available in full text or could not be fetched, so Ukraine/NATO relies on secondary reports; the most recent view (2023) favoured Ukraine in NATO, reversing his 2014 position. Views of the 1957 book (strategy and limited war) were set against his later practice where they differ.

Merged with an independent claude-haiku-5-5 audit: 5 answers taken from it, 12 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-haiku-5-5 notes: Changes of view: on Ukraine he said in 2014 that Ukraine should not join NATO and should be a bridge between East and West (s1); in December 2016 he advised accepting Crimea as Russian; in May 2022 he urged a return to the pre-invasion lines (s2); in January 2023 he called NATO membership for Ukraine an appropriate outcome (s7). The most recent clear position (2023) is used for NATO and Ukraine statements, and the 2022 territorial advice is recorded as low-confidence because a July 2022 interview points the other way (reported in Wikipedia). Contested: Chile 1970-73, Cambodia, Argentina 1976, Angola 1975. Not read in full: Diplomacy (1994), World Order (2014), On China (2011), White House Years, Years of Upheaval, and NSSM 200 (1974, population): archive.org full texts returned 401/404 to the downloader, and their positions were not answered except where cited above. Null answers on population, Holocaust, Israel-Palestinian and US domestic economics reflect the sources reachable in this session, not a verdict.
